title: How a Horse Flu Outbreak Spurred an Early Animal Rights Crusade - Nautilus
gist: Excerpt from Lee Alan Dugatkin's book on the 1872 New York equine influenza epizootic, which sickened thousands of the city's horses and, per the subhead, gave the ASPCA's founder a moral argument for animal protection.

insights.claim: In October 1872 the New York Herald reported 7,000 city horses stricken with catarrhal fever in 24 hours, warning of millions of dollars of horseflesh at stake and disruption to local traffic.
insights.speaker: Lee Alan Dugatkin
insights.so_what: Historical case of a disease outbreak crippling a city's core transport/energy input.
insights.quote: Seven Thousand Horses in the City Stricken with Catarrhal Fever During the Past Twenty-Four Hours

insights.claim: The reporter believed the 7,000 figure was an underestimate, with horses from poor costermongers' sheds to millionaires' stables falling ill alike.
insights.speaker: Lee Alan Dugatkin
insights.so_what: Pandemics in critical infrastructure inputs hit across wealth tiers.
insights.quote: if anything, the seven-thousand figure in the headline was an underestimate
insights.locator: The reporter who penned the story

insights.claim: The 1872 epizootic gave the ASPCA's young founder a powerful moral argument for animal protection, spurring an early animal-rights crusade.
insights.speaker: Lee Alan Dugatkin
insights.so_what: Crises can catalyze lasting regulatory and social movements.
insights.locator: How a Horse Flu Outbreak Spurred
